group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department late yesterday evening after two days of fever, shaking chills, and a progressively wetter cough that produced rusty-tinged sputum; over the prior twelve hours she also noticed pleuritic discomfort along the right posterior chest wall that forced her to sleep propped up in a recliner. Wanting the clinical team to evaluate her baseline state, she withheld her usual morning medications—carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, low-dose furosemide, spironolactone, and lactulose—and did not take acetaminophen, use any inhalers, or turn on the supplemental oxygen concentrator that had been prescribed for a brief hypoxemic episode during last year’s influenza but has not been used since. She drove herself the forty-five minutes from her rural home, stopping only once because a bout of coughing left her short of breath. Past history is notable for long-standing systolic dysfunction attributed to anthracycline exposure during chemotherapy for a breast carcinoma resected twelve years ago; the most recent outpatient echocardiogram three months earlier documented a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 30 % with mild functional mitral regurgitation and chronically elevated right-sided pressures. In addition, she carries a diagnosis of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis with bridging fibrosis discovered eight years ago on biopsy; follow-up transient elastography nine months earlier was unchanged, and baseline labs have shown normal bilirubin with only mild transaminase elevations. There is no record of chronic kidney impairment, and a comprehensive metabolic panel from her cardiology visit six weeks ago demonstrated a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL. She quit a twenty-pack-year cigarette habit a decade ago, drinks no alcohol because of her liver condition, and has never used recreational drugs. Immunizations are current, including the latest inactivated influenza dose administered at a pharmacy this past autumn and both pneumococcal formulations. On roll-in she sat upright on the stretcher, conversing in full sentences and correctly stating her name, the exact date, and the reason for coming in. Skin was warm and mildly diaphoretic with brisk capillary refill; sclera were anicteric, and there was no asterixis. Jugular venous pulsation reached about 4 cm above the sternal angle while she reclined at 45°, consistent with prior cardiology notes, and trace bilateral ankle edema was present. Pre-intervention vital signs obtained on ambient air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.4 °C, regular pulse 76 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead telemetry, right-arm blood pressure 157/86 mm Hg verified manually, respirations 21 breaths per minute with slightly increased thoracoabdominal excursion but no visible accessory muscle use, and fingertip pulse oximetry 91 % while seated. Cardiac auscultation revealed a soft third heart sound in addition to normal S1 and S2 but no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination disclosed markedly decreased breath sounds and stony dull percussion over the lower half of the right hemithorax with faint egophony just above that zone; inspiratory crackles were appreciated in the adjacent middle lobe region, and the left lung transmitted vesicular airflow without adventitious sounds. The abdomen was distended to a small degree by longstanding ascites but remained nontender with preserved bowel sounds; the liver edge was palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and was smooth, and there was no splenomegaly. A focused neurologic screen showed equal reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, 5/5 strength in all extremities, fluent speech, and normal rapid alternating movements without flapping tremor. Finger-stick glucose obtained before phlebotomy read 113 mg/dL. Peripheral venous blood was drawn within ten minutes of bay entry, preceding any saline flushes larger than the 2 mL used to lock the catheter. The basic metabolic panel returned sodium 129 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. A complete blood count showed leukocytes 14.2 × 10⁹/L with 88 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 43 %, hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, and platelets 134 × 10⁹/L—her usual baseline for thrombocytopenia related to portal hypertension. An arterial sample from the left radial artery, obtained while she continued to breathe room air, revealed pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, PaO₂ 72 mm Hg, and a calculated bicarbonate of 20 mEq/L, consistent with a mild hypoxemia and an acid–base profile near physiologic. Serum lactate returned at 1.9 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin I was below the analytic threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph completed before any therapy demonstrated a moderate homogeneous opacity in the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and a meniscus-shaped fluid level layering laterally, obscuring the right costophrenic recess; cardiomediastinal contours were unchanged from a study two months prior, and there was cephalization of the pulmonary vasculature similar to earlier films. Electrocardiography displayed normal sinus rhythm at 77 beats per minute with low-voltage QRS complexes and nonspecific ST-T changes but no acute ischemic pattern. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, an induced sputum sample, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were dispatched prior to any antimicrobial, diuretic, bronchodilator, vasopressor, or supplemental oxygen order. Up to the moment this narrative is dictated she has received no intravenous fluids, antipyretics, or other medications beyond the minimal heparinized saline required for line patency, ensuring that every vital sign, laboratory value, and imaging finding cited above reflects her untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
1. Demographics: for a woman, age minus 10 gives 62 − 10 = 52. Living at home adds 0.
2. Comorbidities: systolic heart failure = 10; chronic liver disease (biopsy-proven steatohepatitis with fibrosis) = 20. Breast cancer resected 12 years ago without reported recurrence is not active or recent neoplastic disease = 0. No cerebrovascular or renal disease documented = 0 each.
3. Examination: alert, RR 21 (<30/min), systolic BP 157 (≥90 mm Hg), temperature 38.4 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 76 (<125/min) = 0 each.
4. Tests: arterial pH 7.34 (<7.35) = 30; sodium 129 (<130 mEq/L) = 20. BUN 18 (<30 mg/dL), glucose 113 (<250 mg/dL), and hematocrit 43% (≥30%) = 0 each. Room-air PaO₂ 72 mm Hg and saturation 91% do not meet the <60 mm Hg or <90% oxygenation cutoff = 0. The right-sided meniscus and obscured costophrenic recess indicate pleural effusion = 10.
Total = 52 + 10 + 20 + 30 + 20 + 10 = 142.
Final answer: 142
